claims.claim: Email marketing is a type of direct marketing that is highly personal and designed to build relationships with consumers; marketers use email to communicate promotions about products and share relevant content (OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.1).

Email marketing is known as permission-based marketing: marketers get consent before sending a promotional message, subscribers opt in, and they can opt out, typically by clicking an unsubscribe link (OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.1).

Marketers generally send two types of emails: transactional emails, which follow an action such as a purchase or return (order confirmation, shipping update), and marketing emails, which are promotional and typically carry an offer (OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.1).

The CAN-SPAM Act sets the rules for commercial email in the United States and covers all commercial messages — any email whose primary purpose is advertising or promoting a commercial product or service — not just bulk email (FTC).

Under CAN-SPAM, senders must honor opt-out requests within 10 business days; the opt-out mechanism must work for at least 30 days after a message is sent; and once someone opts out, the sender may not sell or transfer that address (FTC).

CAN-SPAM requires accurate header information, truthful subject lines, a clear disclosure that the message is an advertisement, and a valid physical postal address in commercial messages; each separate email in violation is subject to a penalty (up to $46,517 per email per the FTC's compliance guide, a figure adjusted over time) (FTC).

Email engagement is measured with open and click rates — companies can measure emails opened and clicked — and email content is expected to be concise with a clear, easy-to-find call to action (OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.2).

An email list is an owned channel — the brand reaches subscribers directly — while social media reach depends on platforms that control which followers see a post; email is one of the owned channels brands use to deliver content directly to an audience (OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.2; CMI).

conflictingEvidence.issue: CAN-SPAM does not require senders to obtain permission before sending the first commercial message — the law governs how messages are sent and requires honoring opt-outs — while OpenStax describes email marketing as permission-based marketing requiring consent. These are not in conflict when separated: permission is the practice standard of the channel, CAN-SPAM is the U.S. legal floor of honoring opt-outs.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both, factually and with attribution: the opt-in standard is presented as the permission-based marketing practice (OpenStax), and CAN-SPAM is presented as the legal minimum (FTC), explicitly noting the law does not mandate opt-in.

sourceRecords.title: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A government source (per subject source-map). ftc.gov blocks automated access, so the page was read via a Wayback Machine capture of the canonical URL dated 2022-03-10. Supports: CAN-SPAM as the U.S. law setting the rules for commercial email; coverage of all commercial messages (primary purpose = commercial advertisement or promotion of a commercial product or service), not just bulk email; requirements — accurate From/To/Reply-To and routing information, no deceptive subject lines, clear and conspicuous disclosure that the message is an ad, a valid physical postal address, a clear and conspicuous opt-out explanation with a return email address or easy web-based way to opt out; opt-out mechanism must work at least 30 days after sending; opt-outs honored within 10 business days; no fee, no extra personal information, and no steps beyond a reply or single web page to opt out; no selling or transferring addresses after opt-out; penalties up to $46,517 per separate email in violation (figure per the guide; penalty amounts are adjusted over time). Also supports the honest nuance: CAN-SPAM does not require senders to get permission before the first message — the opt-in standard is the permission-based marketing practice, stated as such in the lesson. Requirements paraphrased with attribution; no page wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 16.1 Traditional Direct Marketing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A textbook (per subject source-map). openstax.org blocks curl, so the section was read via a Wayback Machine capture dated 2024-05-24. Supports: email marketing as a type of direct marketing that is highly personal and designed to build relationships with consumers; marketers use email to communicate promotions about products and share relevant content; email marketing as permission-based marketing — consent required before sending promotional messages, opt-in, opt-out via unsubscribe link or reply; consumers typically opt in when placing an online order or in exchange for value (exclusive discounts, webinars, free trials); two email types — transactional (order confirmation, shipping updates) and marketing (promotional offers, coupon codes, free shipping); email marketing platforms (e.g., Mailchimp) as the standard tool; newsletters as audience-catered email products. Definitions paraphrased with attribution; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 16.2 Social Media and Mobile Marketing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A textbook; already registered (id reused with identical URL). Read via a Wayback Machine capture dated 2026-05-10. Supports: mobile-friendly emails whose images, text, and links display well on mobile; subject lines that capture attention and paint a benefit; concise emails with a clear, easy-to-find call to action (buttons with actionable language); companies can measure emails opened and clicked; social media marketing defined as using platforms to deliver content, with brands lacking complete control over the message and reach depending on platform algorithms and rules. Paraphrased with attribution.
